title: Polyloglogarithmic suffix-array access in compact space
formal:
Do there exist two deterministic finite word-RAM programs \(P,Q\), integers \(a,c\ge1\) and \(d\ge8\), and constants \(C,K>0\), such that the following holds simultaneously for every integer \(n\ge2\), every binary string \(T\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), and every rank \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\)?
The preprocessing program \(P\), given \(n\) and the packed bits of \(T\), constructs a static index \(I_T\) in at most \(K(n+2)^a\) operations. Given only \(n,i,I_T\), the query program \(Q\) returns the exact value \(\operatorname{SA}_T[i]\) in at most
\[
K\bigl(1+\log_2\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^c
\]
operations. At every point of a query, the index and all query working storage together use at most \(Cn\) bits in the model below. The same programs and constants must work for every input length; all bounds are worst-case.
definitions:
The string \(T\) has positions \(0,\ldots,n-1\). Its nonempty suffix at position \(j\) is \(T[j]T[j+1]\cdots T[n-1]\). Lexicographic order compares the first unequal symbols using \(0<1\); when one string is a proper prefix of the other, the shorter string is smaller. The suffix array \(\operatorname{SA}_T\) is the unique permutation of the positions such that these suffixes, in that order, are lexicographically increasing. There is no empty suffix in the array and no sentinel symbol in the input. A suffix-array query translates a rank into the corresponding starting position. It is not the inverse query that translates a position into its rank.

Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). The preprocessing input gives \(n\) in one word and the bits of \(T\) packed consecutively into \(\lceil n/w\rceil\) words, with unused final bits zero. The programs have finite code independent of \(n\) and the input, using finitely many fixed integer constants. Word reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor cost one operation each. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Addresses and values fit in words; operations on multiple words pay for their constituent instructions. There are no random operations, nonuniform advice strings, free lookup tables or input-dependent oracles.

The output index is a finite bit string stored in consecutive words with zero padding. Its length and any metadata, pointers, retained text copies, generated tables and other stored information are part of the index-space charge. A query may read the index but cannot change it. Its separate workspace and registers start without information from earlier queries, and all storage used by the query counts toward the same \(Cn\)-bit bound. Word padding counts as stored bits. The externally provided \(n\) and \(i\), and the returned answer, occupy only a constant number of words; they do not contain any other input-dependent information. The original text is unavailable to \(Q\) unless its representation is included in \(I_T\).

All preprocessing operations, including producing tables and writing the index, count toward the polynomial construction bound. Preprocessing can use temporary storage beyond \(Cn\) bits, subject to the word-RAM address space; this temporary storage is discarded and unavailable during queries. All query computation and writing of its answer count toward its time bound. There is no restriction to repetitive texts, a small set of queries or an average over input strings. The exponent \(c\) is a single constant chosen with the programs, not a function of \(n\); the same applies to \(a,d,C,K\).

context_blocks.text: The retained threshold \(O((1+\log\log(n+2))^c)\), binary alphabet and polynomial deterministic preprocessing are editorial specifications of the compact suffix-array frontier. They are not a verbatim question from Thankachan. His September 2026 revision discusses barriers to \(\log^{o(1)}n\) forward-query time; the card selects a particular stronger upper-bound target within that regime.

The 2026 construction paper reports compact suffix-array representations with \(O(n)\) bits and \(O(\log^\varepsilon n)\) query time for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), for binary texts. Selecting a smaller fixed \(\varepsilon\) is different from obtaining one fixed power of \(\log\log n\).

The separate August 2026 lower-bound preprint states that deterministic suffix-array structures for binary strings of length at most \(N\), with \(O(N)\) bits and \(\Theta(\log N)\)-bit cells, require \(\Omega(\log\log N/\log\log\log N)\) worst-case probes. This excludes constant time in that model, but remains compatible with the polyloglogarithmic target. The detailed theorem, rather than just its simplified introduction, explicitly specifies determinism.

The companion August 2026 preprint claims \(O(1)\)-time inverse suffix-array queries in \(O(n)\) bits for binary texts. Its forward suffix-array tradeoffs have different space and query-time factors. The inverse-access result does not provide the requested rank-to-position access. These recent preprint statements were checked for scope; their complete proofs were not independently certified in this review.

The June 2020 paper gives a compact text index with sublinear deterministic construction time and pattern-occurrence queries. Construction speed and pattern searching provide relevant history, but are different guarantees from the forward-access threshold fixed here.

Thankachan’s final question in Section 7 concerns reducing auxiliary suffix-tree/array space while retaining polylogarithmic query times. This card does not attribute its particular polyloglogarithmic threshold to that concluding question.

why: A text contains enough information to determine the full suffix order, but explicitly storing every starting position costs an extra logarithmic factor in bits. This question asks whether that factor can be removed while each rank-to-position lookup takes only a fixed polynomial in the double logarithm of the text length.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that the programs and constants specified above exist, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of that proposition. An upper bound with superlinear bit space, a result only for inverse suffix-array access, an expected-time bound, or a lower bound that only rules out constant query time does not settle this exact target.

progress.text: The CPM paper gives compact text indexing with sublinear deterministic construction and packed pattern-search bounds.
The lower-bound preprint states a nonconstant deterministic cell-probe lower bound for compact forward suffix-array access.
The companion preprint claims constant-time compact inverse access and deterministic constructions for several forward-access tradeoffs.
Thankachan’s revised paper discusses the forward-access barrier and the newly separated inverse-access result; its final open question concerns auxiliary space.

status_note: The exact polyloglogarithmic threshold remains an editorial specialization of the compact forward-access frontier, rather than a verbatim dated source question. The checked August and September 2026 manuscripts discuss nearby upper and lower bounds, but neither constant-time inverse access nor the nonconstant forward-access lower bound settles this target. A bounded later-work review through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. Status is uncertain for this precise specialization; the recent manuscripts have not received an independent full proof audit.

category_assignment.reason: The main target is a general string-processing, compressed-representation or sequence-comparison primitive.

sentences: A suffix array orders all nonempty suffixes of a binary string lexicographically.
A query asks for the starting position of the suffix with a specified rank.
The target is one deterministic static index family with linear bit space, including query workspace, and polynomial preprocessing.
Each query must return its exact answer in worst-case time bounded by one fixed power of the double logarithm of the string length.
Recent inverse-access and nonconstant lower-bound claims concern nearby thresholds and do not establish this particular forward-access guarantee.
